item.text: [{"taxonId":48323,"summary":"A plant genus in the Goodeniaceae, with about 130 species and an unusually broad distribution outside Australia for its family. Australian members often range from herbs to shrubs and have dry fruits, whereas almost all species outside Australia have fleshy fruits and are often tall shrubs or trees.","humanEdibility":"unknown","edibilityNote":null,"evidence":{"summary":["s1:p2","s1:p3","s1:p4"],"humanEdibility":[]}},{"taxonId":48353,"summary":"A widespread genus of shrubs and dwarf shrubs found worldwide except Australia and Antarctica, mostly in cooler parts of the Northern Hemisphere. Its species typically favour acidic soils, and the fruits of many species are eaten by people, including blueberries, cranberries and bilberries.","humanEdibility":"yes","edibilityNote":"The fruits of many species are eaten; commercially important examples include blueberries, cranberries, bilberries, lingonberries and huckleberries.","evidence":{"summary":["s1:p2","s1:p11"],"humanEdibility":["s1:p2"]}},{"taxonId":48368,"summary":"A moss genus in the Encalyptaceae, broadly distributed across the Americas, Europe, Asia, Africa and Australia, as well as Madagascar and New Zealand. It comprises 34 species and is commonly called extinguisher moss.","humanEdibility":"unknown","edibilityNote":null,"evidence":{"summary":["s1:p1"],"humanEdibility":[]}},{"taxonId":48379,"summary":"A genus of herbaceous perennial flowering plants native from the Himalayas to eastern Asia, including China, Japan, the Philippines and Taiwan. They spread by creeping underground stems and bear showy white or yellow flowers, usually purple-spotted, with six often backward-curving flower parts.","humanEdibility":"unknown","edibilityNote":null,"evidence":{"summary":["s1:p1","s1:p2"],"humanEdibility":[]}},{"taxonId":48385,"summary":"A genus of largely evergreen perennials native to North America, except Heuchera sichotensis, which is native to the Russian Far East. Their long-stalked, hand-shaped lobed leaves rise from thick, woody rootstocks.","humanEdibility":"unknown","edibilityNote":null,"evidence":{"summary":["s1:p1","s1:p2"],"humanEdibility":[]}},{"taxonId":48448,"summary":"A tall annual cereal grass domesticated by Indigenous peoples in southern Mexico about 9,000 years ago from wild teosinte. It bears pollen-producing tassels above female ears whose kernels may be yellow, white or many other colours. The grain is a worldwide staple used for foods including tortillas, tamales, polenta and hominy grits.","humanEdibility":"yes","edibilityNote":"The kernels are eaten fresh or processed into staples such as cornmeal, tortillas, tamales, polenta and hominy grits.","evidence":{"summary":["s1:p2","s1:p5","s1:p8","s1:p9"],"humanEdibility":["s1:p72"]}},{"taxonId":48449,"summary":"A grass genus whose only domesticated taxon is Zea mays subsp. mays, widely used for human food and animal feed; all remaining taxa are wild and collectively called teosintes.","humanEdibility":"yes","edibilityNote":"Only the domesticated taxon Zea mays subsp. mays is documented here as extensively used for human food.","evidence":{"summary":["s1:p2"],"humanEdibility":["s1:p2"]}},{"taxonId":48517,"summary":"A genus of flowering plants native to the Americas and cultivated worldwide for edible fruits known as peppers. Its fruits vary greatly in colour, shape and size. Most species produce capsaicin, causing a burning sensation, although the bell pepper cultivar of Capsicum annuum has none.","humanEdibility":"yes","edibilityNote":"The fruits can be eaten raw or cooked and may also be dried, pickled, frozen or made into sauces.","evidence":{"summary":["s1:p2","s1:p14","s1:p31","s1:p34"],"humanEdibility":["s1:p37","s1:p39"]}},{"taxonId":48528,"summary":"A genus of deciduous shrubs native to North and Central America, except Symphoricarpos sinensis, which is native to western China. It bears closely packed clusters of soft berries that may be white, pink, red or, in S. sinensis, blackish purple. White berries reveal a sparkling, snow-like interior and crack when stepped on.","humanEdibility":"unknown","edibilityNote":null,"evidence":{"summary":["s1:p2","s1:p4","s1:p5"],"humanEdibility":[]}},{"taxonId":48592,"summary":"A biennial vegetable known only from cultivation, with no known wild ancestral form; its geographic origin is uncertain and domestication likely occurred in West or Central Asia. It forms a layered bulb below a fan of hollow bluish-green leaves, and bulb swelling is triggered by day length. The bulb and young plants are eaten raw, cooked or pickled, while chopping can release eye-irritating chemicals.","humanEdibility":"yes","edibilityNote":"Mature bulbs and young whole plants are eaten raw or cooked; bulbs are also pickled or made into chutneys.","evidence":{"summary":["s1:p3","s1:p4","s1:p5","s1:p15"],"humanEdibility":["s1:p5","s1:p25"]}}]
